verifiedFacts.claim: Butch Vig says the backing track for "Come As You Are" was recorded quickly and that the bass was triple-tracked, including regular, octave, and DBX sub-harmonic parts.

sourceRefs.label: MOJO interview transcript (Live Nirvana, with permission)
sourceRefs.title: Titanic! The Nevermind Recording Sessions — MOJO #54 (May 1998)
sourceRefs.sourceIdentity: livenirvana.com|MOJO #54 Peter Henderson interview with Butch Vig
sourceRefs.extract: Come As You Are Kurt Cobain's message to his disenfranchised audience was simple: he would accept them as they were, and he offered them no threat. His lyrics were more or less complete by the time Vig first heard the song, recorded in a rehearsal on an old boom box. Vig: "The backing track was very quick. We actually triple-tracked the bass: a regular bass, then Chris played an octave bass, then he tuned the bass strangely and ran it through a DBX sub-harmonic effect. We were trying to make the bass sound like a 12-string."

limitations: Only the source-backed production/session statement is retained; no independent listening or audio-analysis claim is made.

verifiedFacts.claim: MOJO's session account says "Lithium" was relatively difficult to record: Dave Grohl tracked drums to a click, with bass, guitars, and quieter guitar parts added separately.

sourceRefs.label: MOJO interview transcript (Live Nirvana, with permission)
sourceRefs.title: Titanic! The Nevermind Recording Sessions — MOJO #54 (May 1998)
sourceRefs.sourceIdentity: livenirvana.com|MOJO #54 Peter Henderson interview with Butch Vig
sourceRefs.extract: Lithium proved relatively difficult to record, partly because Cobain insisted on an even tempo, keeping the same pace for the raucous choruses and the more thoughtful, guitar-led section. Grohl therefore recorded the drums to a click track, with the bass and guitars added later. The quieter guitar parts were also done separately.

limitations: Only the source-backed production/session statement is retained; no independent listening or audio-analysis claim is made.

verifiedFacts.claim: Butch Vig says the 17-bar abstract section in "Drain You" retained sounds Kurt Cobain made with objects including squeaky ducks, percussion, and an aerosol during vocal passes.

sourceRefs.label: MOJO interview transcript (Live Nirvana, with permission)
sourceRefs.title: Titanic! The Nevermind Recording Sessions — MOJO #54 (May 1998)
sourceRefs.sourceIdentity: livenirvana.com|MOJO #54 Peter Henderson interview with Butch Vig
sourceRefs.extract: Drain You is essentially a conventional love song with the unconventional subject of two babies lying in a hospital bed; the title refers to how each will drain the other of infection. Vig: "Instead of concocting a guitar solo, every time Kurt did a vocal pass he would run to the side of the room at that part of the song and pick something up - squeaky ducks, percussion things or an aerosol. It became an abstract part for 17 bars. We just left them all in on the mix."

limitations: Only the source-backed production/session statement is retained; no independent listening or audio-analysis claim is made.

sourceRefs.extract: On A Plain Vig: "A great pop song. A really new one. It took a few takes to get it." verifiedFacts.claim: Butch Vig says the foundation of "Something In The Way" was recorded with Kurt Cobain singing and playing quietly on the control-room couch, after which harmonies, bass, and drums were added.

sourceRefs.label: MOJO interview transcript (Live Nirvana, with permission)
sourceRefs.title: Titanic! The Nevermind Recording Sessions — MOJO #54 (May 1998)
sourceRefs.sourceIdentity: livenirvana.com|MOJO #54 Peter Henderson interview with Butch Vig
sourceRefs.extract: Something In The Way Vig: "This was written just a week before recording and was by far the most difficult track to record. We spent most of a day trying to record it as a band, working out different drum parts. Kurt came into the control room and said, 'I can't get into this at all.' I said, 'How do you hear it then?' and he sat down on the couch and was hardly mumbling the vocal, playing the guitar so quietly. So I said, 'Everybody shut up,' turned the fans and everything off and brought a couple of mics into the control room. He kind of laid on the couch and I gave him an acoustic mic and a vocal mic and he recorded it in the control room. Then he put the harmonies on and we went back and did the bass, which Chris found very hard. We then recorded the drums in studio B. It almost killed Dave to play so quietly.

verifiedFacts.claim: Butch Vig says Nirvana launched into "Endless, Nameless" after completing a frustrating "Lithium" take, and that Kurt Cobain smashed his left-handed Mosrite during the performance.

sourceRefs.label: MOJO interview transcript (Live Nirvana, with permission)
sourceRefs.title: Titanic! The Nevermind Recording Sessions — MOJO #54 (May 1998)
sourceRefs.sourceIdentity: livenirvana.com|MOJO #54 Peter Henderson interview with Butch Vig
sourceRefs.extract: Endless, Nameless Vig: "Lithium took quite a while. It was a long day and Kurt became very frustrated, and after we finally got a take, they launched into Endless Nameless and Kurt fucking went ballistic. He was screaming so hard I swore to God he had blown his vocal cords out and in the middle of it he smashed his guitar up. It was the only left-handed Mosrite he had but he was so pissed off that he didn't care. He went back in and screamed some more. We spent the next day going round LA trying to track down another left-handed Mosrite."

limitations: Only the source-backed production/session statement is retained; no independent listening or audio-analysis claim is made.
